learn.hook: Imagine a pet that turns your bathtub into a water park every single day!
points: In 'Mijbil the Otter', Gavin Maxwell brings home an otter from Iraq and names him Mijbil (Mij).
Mij turned out to be of a kind of otter not known to science before, so it was named after Maxwell: Maxwell's otter.
Subject-verb agreement: a singular subject takes a singular verb (The otter swims); a plural subject takes a plural verb (Otters swim).
Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb. With 'each', 'every', 'either of', 'neither of' and 'one of the ...', use a singular verb.
With 'either...or' or 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. With 'along with' or 'as well as', it agrees with the first subject.

example.q: Passage: Our puppy, Laddoo, and our old cat, Mishri, share the sunny corner of the verandah. Neither of them likes the noisy mixer. Every morning, the pair races to the kitchen when the milk boils. Why does the passage say 'Neither of them likes', not 'like'?
steps: The subject is 'Neither of them'.
'Neither' means not this one and not that one, taken one at a time.
So it is treated as singular and takes 'likes'.
example.answer: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb, so 'likes' is correct.

learn.reallife: Board exam gap-filling and editing questions often test agreement: 'Each of the students has a book.'

items.text: Laddoo and Mishri ___ the sunny corner.
Each of the otters ___ a name.
One of my pets ___ a parrot.
Neither the cat nor the puppies ___ the mixer.
The teacher, along with her students, ___ visiting the zoo.

games.title: Otter and agreement facts
items: Gavin Maxwell brought Mijbil from Iraq.
He got the otter while in southern Iraq.
Mij's kind of otter was named after Gavin Maxwell.
It became known as Maxwell's otter.
'Every boy and girl were present' is correct.
'Every' takes a singular verb: 'Every boy and girl was present.'
With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
'Either Ravi or his sisters are coming.'
'The pair races' is wrong because pair means two.
'Pair' is one unit here, so a singular verb is fine.

quiz.q: From which country did Gavin Maxwell bring Mijbil the otter?
quiz.explain: Maxwell got Mij in southern Iraq and later took him to London.
steps: Gavin Maxwell got Mij in southern Iraq.
He later took him to London.
Answer: Iraq
quiz.mistake: Confuses where Mij came from with where he was taken

quiz.q: Why was Mij's kind of otter named after Gavin Maxwell?
options: Maxwell had caught every otter in Iraq
It had not been known to science before
It was the biggest otter in the world
It was born in Maxwell's house
quiz.explain: It was a new race of otter, so it was named Maxwell's otter.
steps: Mij's kind of otter was a race not known to science before.
So it was named after Maxwell: Maxwell's otter.
Answer: It had not been known to science before
quiz.mistake: Thinks animals are named after owners of pets

quiz.q: Passage: Our puppy, Laddoo, and our old cat, Mishri, share the sunny corner of the verandah. Neither of them likes the noisy mixer. Every morning, the pair races to the kitchen when the milk boils. Choose the correct verb: 'Neither of them ___ the noisy mixer.'
quiz.explain: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb.
steps: 'Neither of them' refers to one at a time.
'Neither of' takes a singular verb: likes.
Answer: likes
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'them' makes the subject plural

quiz.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Laddoo and Mishri ___ the corner of the verandah.'
quiz.explain: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb.
steps: Two subjects are joined by 'and': Laddoo and Mishri.
Subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb: share.
Answer: share
quiz.mistake: Matches the verb only with the nearest noun

quiz.q: Choose the correct verb: 'One of my pets ___ a parrot.'
quiz.explain: The subject is 'one', so the verb is singular.
steps: The real subject is 'one' (not 'pets').
'One' is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
Answer: is
quiz.mistake: Agrees the verb with 'pets' instead of 'one'

quiz.q: Choose the correct verb: 'The teacher, along with her students, ___ visiting the zoo.'
quiz.explain: With 'along with', the verb agrees with the first subject, 'the teacher'.
steps: With 'along with', the verb agrees with the first subject.
'The teacher' is singular, so 'is'.
Answer: is
quiz.mistake: Counts the students as part of the subject

quiz.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Either the cats or the dog ___ broken the vase.'
quiz.explain: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the dog'.
steps: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
The nearer subject is 'the dog' (singular): has.
Answer: has
quiz.mistake: Agrees with the first subject 'cats'

quiz.q: Passage: Our puppy, Laddoo, and our old cat, Mishri, share the sunny corner of the verandah. Neither of them likes the noisy mixer. Every morning, the pair races to the kitchen when the milk boils. What do the pets do when the milk boils?
options: They run away from the mixer
quiz.explain: The last line says the pair races to the kitchen.
steps: The last line says what happens when the milk boils.
'The pair races to the kitchen.'
Answer: They race to the kitchen
quiz.mistake: Mixes up two details from the passage

teach.ask: Gappu: Is it 'Each of the birds sing' or 'Each of the birds sings'? My head is spinning!
teach.praise: Phew, chirp! 'Each' is singular, so 'Each of the birds sings.' My head has stopped spinning!
teach.nudge: Is 'each' about one or many? What kind of verb does it need?

revise.summary: Gavin Maxwell brings home an otter from Iraq, Mijbil, whose kind was new to science and so was named Maxwell's otter. We also learn the rules of subject-verb agreement.
focus: Recall where Mij came from and why his kind was named after Maxwell.
Apply agreement rules for 'and', 'each', 'one of', 'neither of'.
Apply the rules for either...or, neither...nor, along with, as well as.
remember: A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.
Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb; each, every, either of, neither of, one of the ... take a singular verb.
either...or / neither...nor: agree with the nearer subject; along with / as well as: agree with the first subject.
traps: Don't let 'them' in 'Neither of them' make the verb plural: 'Neither of them likes'.
Don't agree with 'pets' in 'One of my pets is'; the subject is 'one'.
With 'along with', don't count the added people: 'The teacher, along with her students, is'.

learn.hook: Otters slide, splash, juggle and even sulk. Watching them is like watching a comedy show!
points: Mij loved water: he played and splashed in the bath, and was full of playful energy.
He travelled to London by plane, packed in a box, and later made the flat his playground.
Strong, precise verbs describe behaviour vividly: a snake slithers, a duck waddles, a tiger prowls, a mouse scurries.
Adverbs tell how an action is done: The otter swam gracefully. Many are formed by adding -ly to an adjective (graceful → gracefully).
Careful observers note what an animal does, when and how often, without exaggerating.

example.q: Passage: The otter on the Chambal bank slid down the mud, splashed into the river, and bobbed up with a fish, chirping happily. Then it rolled over and over on the warm sand. Which words show that the otter is playful and happy?
steps: 'slid down the mud' and 'rolled over and over' are play actions.
'splashed' and 'bobbed up' show it enjoying the water.
'chirping happily': the adverb 'happily' tells us its mood.
example.answer: slid, splashed, rolled over and over, and 'chirping happily'.

learn.reallife: Smooth-coated otters live in Indian rivers like the Chambal. Wildlife scientists record their behaviour to protect them.

quiz.q: In 'Mijbil the Otter', what did Mij love most?
quiz.explain: Mij spent hours splashing and playing in water.
steps: Mij spent hours splashing and playing in water.
That was what he loved most.
Answer: Playing in water
quiz.mistake: Assumes typical pet behaviour

quiz.q: How did Mij travel to London?
options: By plane, packed in a box
quiz.explain: Mij was packed in a box and flown to London.
steps: Mij had to travel from Iraq to London.
He was packed in a box and flown by plane.
Answer: By plane, packed in a box
quiz.mistake: Guesses a common way of moving pets

quiz.q: Passage: The otter on the Chambal bank slid down the mud, splashed into the river, and bobbed up with a fish, chirping happily. Then it rolled over and over on the warm sand. What sound did the otter make?
quiz.explain: The passage says it was 'chirping happily'.
steps: The passage says the otter bobbed up 'chirping happily'.
So it chirped.
Answer: It chirped
quiz.mistake: Assumes a sound from a different animal

quiz.q: Which verb best describes how a snake moves?
quiz.explain: Snakes slide along the ground: they slither.
steps: Snakes have no legs and slide along the ground.
That movement is called slithering.
Answer: Slithers
quiz.mistake: Mixes up movement verbs of different animals

quiz.q: Which verb best describes how a duck walks?
quiz.explain: Ducks walk with a side-to-side sway: they waddle.
steps: Ducks walk with a side-to-side sway.
That is waddling.
Answer: Waddles
quiz.mistake: Picks a verb for a different animal

quiz.q: Which verb best describes a tiger moving quietly while hunting?
quiz.explain: To prowl is to move quietly and secretly, looking for prey.
steps: A hunting tiger moves quietly and secretly.
That is prowling.
Answer: Prowls
quiz.mistake: Does not know the precise meaning of 'prowl'

quiz.q: Choose the adverb: 'The otter swam ___ through the water.'
quiz.explain: An adverb describes the verb 'swam'; graceful + -ly = gracefully.
steps: The word describes how the otter swam — a verb — so we need an adverb.
graceful + -ly = gracefully.
Answer: gracefully
quiz.mistake: Uses an adjective to describe a verb

quiz.q: Which word means 'playful and full of fun'?
quiz.explain: Frolicsome means lively and playful.
steps: Frolicsome means lively and full of fun.
Gloomy, lazy and fierce mean other things.
Answer: Frolicsome
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the sound of the word

teach.ask: Gappu: How do I describe what my friend the otter did today so it sounds exciting, not boring?
teach.praise: Splish-chirp! Strong verbs like 'splashed' and adverbs like 'happily' make my story come alive!
teach.nudge: Which kind of words show actions, and which tell us how an action is done?

revise.summary: Mij loved playing in water and travelled to London by plane, packed in a box. We also use strong, precise verbs and -ly adverbs to describe animal behaviour.
focus: Recall details of Mij's behaviour and journey.
Choose the precise verb for how an animal moves.
Use an adverb, not an adjective, to describe a verb.
remember: A snake slithers, a duck waddles, a tiger prowls, a mouse scurries.
Adverbs tell how an action is done; many add -ly to an adjective (graceful → gracefully).
Careful observers note what an animal does, when and how often, without exaggerating.
traps: Don't use an adjective to describe a verb: 'swam gracefully', not 'swam graceful'.
Don't mix up movement verbs of different animals.

learn.hook: What if fog were a cat that tiptoes into the city and then quietly walks away?
points: 'Fog' by Carl Sandburg compares the fog to a cat: it arrives silently, sits and watches the city, then moves on.
A metaphor says one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as': 'The classroom was a zoo.'
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as': 'He runs like a cheetah.'
An extended metaphor carries one comparison through many lines, as with the fog and the cat.
Personification gives human qualities to non-human things; metaphors often work alongside it.

example.q: Poem: Evening is a grey heron / Standing still on one leg; / It folds the river in its wings / And flies off into the night. What is evening compared to, and is it a simile or a metaphor?
steps: Evening is directly called 'a grey heron'.
There is no 'like' or 'as'.
The comparison continues: it stands, folds its wings and flies off, so it is extended.
example.answer: Evening is compared to a grey heron; it is an (extended) metaphor.

learn.reallife: We use metaphors every day: 'Mumbai never sleeps', 'my brother is a couch potato', 'time is money'.

games.title: Simile or metaphor?
items: The baby slept like a log.
Her voice was as sweet as honey.

games.title: What does the metaphor mean?
pairs: My brother is a couch potato.
lazy, watches a lot of TV

quiz.q: Who wrote the poem 'Fog'?
quiz.explain: 'Fog' is by Carl Sandburg.
steps: 'Fog' is a short poem in this chapter.
It was written by Carl Sandburg.
Answer: Carl Sandburg
quiz.mistake: Mixes up poets of First Flight

quiz.q: In 'Fog', what is the fog compared to?
quiz.explain: The fog moves silently, sits and moves on like a cat.
steps: The fog comes silently, sits looking over the city and moves on.
These are the actions of a cat.
Answer: A cat
quiz.mistake: Guesses a fierce animal

quiz.q: What is a metaphor?
options: A direct comparison that says one thing is another
A word that imitates a sound
quiz.explain: A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as'.
steps: A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as'.
It says one thing is another.
Answer: A direct comparison that says one thing is another
quiz.mistake: Confuses metaphor with simile

quiz.q: 'Her smile is sunshine.' What figure of speech is this?
quiz.explain: It says the smile IS sunshine, with no 'like' or 'as'.
steps: 'Her smile is sunshine' says the smile IS sunshine.
There is no 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor.
Answer: Metaphor
quiz.mistake: Thinks every comparison is a simile

quiz.q: 'He runs like a cheetah.' What figure of speech is this?
quiz.explain: It compares using 'like', so it is a simile.
steps: 'He runs like a cheetah' compares using 'like'.
A comparison with 'like' or 'as' is a simile.
Answer: Simile
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the word 'like'

quiz.q: Poem: Evening is a grey heron / Standing still on one leg; / It folds the river in its wings / And flies off into the night. What is evening compared to?
quiz.explain: Line 1 says 'Evening is a grey heron'.
steps: Line 1 says 'Evening is a grey heron'.
So evening is compared to a grey heron.
Answer: A grey heron
quiz.mistake: Picks another noun from the poem

quiz.q: Why is the comparison in 'Fog' a metaphor rather than a simile?
options: It has a cat in it
quiz.explain: Similes need 'like' or 'as'; the fog is described as a cat directly.
steps: A simile must use 'like' or 'as'.
'Fog' describes the fog as a cat directly, without them — so it is a metaphor.
Answer: It does not use 'like' or 'as'
quiz.mistake: Thinks the subject decides the figure of speech

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a metaphor?
options: The baby slept like a log.
quiz.explain: 'Like a log' uses 'like', so it is a simile.
steps: 'Like a log' uses 'like'.
So 'The baby slept like a log' is a simile, not a metaphor.
Answer: The baby slept like a log.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the word 'like'

teach.ask: Gappu: My teacher said 'Gappu is a little rocket!' I'm not a rocket. What did she mean?
teach.praise: Zoom-chirp! It's a metaphor: she meant I'm fast, without saying 'like'. I am a little rocket!
teach.nudge: Is she comparing you to something? Does she use 'like' or 'as'?

revise.summary: 'Fog' by Carl Sandburg compares the fog to a cat in an extended metaphor. A metaphor says one thing is another, while a simile uses 'like' or 'as'.
focus: Tell a metaphor from a simile.
Explain the extended metaphor of the fog and the cat.
Spot metaphors in new poem lines.
remember: A metaphor says one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as': 'The classroom was a zoo.'
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as': 'He runs like a cheetah.'
An extended metaphor carries one comparison through many lines.
traps: Don't call every comparison a simile; without 'like' or 'as' it is a metaphor.
Don't overlook 'like': 'slept like a log' is a simile, not a metaphor.
The fog is compared to a cat, not a fierce animal.
